stories.headline: 1 killed, 5 hospitalized after truck crashes into Tour de Fat crowd in Fort Collins
stories.summary:
One person was killed and five others were hospitalized after a Chevrolet pickup truck reversed out of a parking spot, struck another vehicle and drove onto a busy sidewalk along the 100 block of West Mountain Avenue in Old Town Fort Collins on Saturday. The crash occurred at 11:44 a.m. during the annual Tour de Fat parade and festival, striking five pedestrians and a tree before coming to a stop.

The driver was also taken to a hospital. Fort Collins Police Services said detectives are investigating the crash, including whether impairment was a factor, and that there is no indication the pedestrians were targeted. The name of the deceased will be released by the Larimer County coroner's office.

Tour de Fat is an annual event hosted by New Belgium Brewery that draws tens of thousands of costumed participants for a bicycle-forward parade through downtown Fort Collins, followed by live music, food and entertainment at the brewery. Proceeds benefit local bike nonprofits. Anyone with information who has not yet spoken to police is asked to contact Officer David Kaes or Officer Kevin Alexander at 970-416-6540.

stories.headline: Update: High E. coli levels confirmed in Arkansas River following 4.25 million-gallon Pueblo sewage spill
stories.summary:
State officials confirmed Friday that water samples from the Arkansas River downstream of Pueblo tested at "extremely high" levels of bacteria, including E. coli, following this week's massive sewage spill from a failed wastewater pipe. The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment issued a public health advisory urging people and animals to avoid all contact with the river from where Fountain Creek enters the Arkansas River in Pueblo through John Martin Reservoir in Hasty.

The advisory covers communities including Blende, Avondale, Fowler, Manzanola, Rocky Ford, La Junta and Las Animas. Residents are warned not to swim, wade, tube, kayak, fish or allow pets or livestock near the water, and not to use untreated river water on raw produce. Testing will continue over coming days, and officials have not yet said how long the advisory will remain in effect.

State officials said there is no evidence the spill affected public drinking water systems, which were notified in time to shut off intakes. About 25% of Aurora's water supply comes from the Arkansas River watershed, but the city diverts water upstream near Buena Vista, well above the affected stretch. Ranches and farms in the Arkansas River Valley covered by FDA produce safety rules have been notified and must ensure any water they use meets quality standards.

stories.headline: Colorado data center power rules draw scrutiny over ratepayer protections, Xcel loophole concerns
stories.summary:
The Colorado Public Utilities Commission is crafting new regulations governing how data centers and other large power consumers connect to Xcel Energy's grid — rules that would be the most comprehensive statewide standards for the booming industry. Xcel estimates demand from data centers and large-load customers could require more than 1,900 megawatts of additional power by 2031, a 31% increase to the utility's current total supply and enough to power 2.1 million homes.

Environmental advocates and local leaders are raising concerns about a potential loophole in the proposed rules that could allow data center costs to be passed on to Xcel's 1.6 million residential and small business customers rather than borne by the companies themselves. The PUC directed Xcel to develop the rules specifically to prevent that cost-shifting, following years of failed attempts by state legislators to pass data center regulations.

Denver has already banned new data center development pending updates to city ordinances, while some other local governments have enacted their own rules. State Sen. Cathy Kipp, a Larimer County Democrat who sponsored failed data center legislation, said the PUC rulemaking is now "the only place left" to establish real protections before costs fall on ordinary ratepayers. Dozens of data centers already operate along the Front Range, with demand accelerating due to artificial intelligence growth and expanding digital infrastructure needs.

stories.headline: U.S. Supreme Court mail-voting ruling creates uncertainty for Colorado elections
stories.summary:
A U.S. Supreme Court ruling on a Trump administration order affecting mail voting has created significant uncertainty for Colorado election administrators heading into the November election cycle. Colorado is one of the nation's leading mail-ballot states, with nearly all voters casting ballots by mail, making federal changes to mail-voting rules particularly consequential for the state.

The ruling adds complexity to an already uncertain election landscape in Colorado, where voters are also set to decide on Initiative 362, a ballot measure that would require mail ballot ID verification. Secretary of State officials have not yet detailed how they will respond to the federal ruling or what operational changes may be required.

The development comes as Colorado's election administration is already under scrutiny following the recent disclosure that the Secretary of State's office exposed confidential voter data for more than 130,000 residents. Election officials and advocacy groups are monitoring the situation as the state approaches key deadlines for November ballot preparation.

stories.headline: Gov. Polis grants pardons to 29 Coloradans convicted of theft, drug and fraud offenses
stories.summary:
Gov. Jared Polis has granted pardons to 29 Coloradans convicted of theft, drug and fraud offenses, the governor's office announced. The pardons represent one of the broader clemency actions taken by the Polis administration and apply to individuals who have already completed their sentences.

A pardon in Colorado does not expunge a criminal record but does restore certain civil rights, including the right to vote, serve on a jury and hold public office. The governor's office did not immediately detail the specific criteria used to select the 29 recipients or whether any of the pardons were connected to broader criminal justice reform efforts.

The action follows ongoing debates in Colorado and nationally about the use of executive clemency to address inequities in the criminal justice system, particularly for nonviolent drug offenses. Colorado has in recent years also pursued broader legislative approaches to criminal justice reform, including changes to drug sentencing laws.

stories.headline: Colorado Dragon Boat Festival returns to Sloan's Lake after 2025 algae-related postponement
stories.summary:
Thousands of paddlers and spectators gathered at Sloan's Lake Park in Denver on Saturday for the annual Colorado Dragon Boat Festival, which returned to its traditional summer dates after an algae bloom forced the event to push back its schedule in 2025. Thirty-nine paddling teams competed in dragon boat races throughout the weekend, with 26 teams taking to the water Saturday in heats of three boats each.

The free two-day festival celebrates Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander culture through racing, food, music and cultural programming. The event, which debuted at Sloan's Lake in 2001, has grown from a one-day gathering of about 16,000 attendees into a two-day festival drawing nearly 200,000 people.

Dragon boat racing has roots in southern China dating back more than 2,000 years, with the modern competitive sport tracing its origins to Hong Kong in the 1970s. The festival was founded by three Denver-area Asian community leaders with the goal of showcasing the city's growing and diverse Asian community to the broader public.

stories.headline: Broncos begin roster cutdown to 53 players, fullback Adam Prentice among moves
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos began trimming their 91-man roster Saturday ahead of the NFL's 4 p.m. Sunday deadline for all teams to reach 53 players. The club waived and released 11 players Saturday, with those transactions set to appear on the league's wire Sunday. Among the moves, defensive tackle Israel Antwine, offensive lineman Foster Sarell, center Lecitus Smith and outside linebacker Ron Stone Jr. were released.

Fullback Adam Prentice, one of the more productive players in Denver's preseason, is set to be released Sunday but has agreed to return immediately to the practice squad. As a vested veteran, Prentice is not subject to the waiver wire and can re-sign with Denver without risk of being claimed. Head coach Sean Payton said the Broncos plan to use similar arrangements with at least one or two other players to protect younger players from the waiver wire.

The Broncos are projected to carry three quarterbacks — Bo Nix, Jarrett Stidham and Sam Ehlinger — along with a backfield of J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey and Jonah Coleman. Tight end remains an area of concern, with Evan Engram expected to lead a group that also includes rookies Justin Joly and Dallen Bentley and veteran Adam Trautman. Denver's next regular-season game is against the Kansas City Chiefs on Monday, Sept. 14.

stories.headline: Colorado high school football: Valor Christian rolls to 2-0, Cherry Creek on bye in Week 1
stories.summary:
Valor Christian improved to 2-0 with a dominant 46-9 victory over Faith Lutheran of Nevada, with quarterback Titus Huard completing 16 of 24 passes for 296 yards and three touchdowns to wide receiver Jackson Coleman, who finished with 194 receiving yards. Running back Roger Garey added 92 rushing yards and two scores. The Eagles are positioning themselves as the top challenger to Cherry Creek, with the two teams set to meet Sept. 18.

Cherry Creek, ranked No. 1 in The Denver Post's preseason top 10, was on bye in Week 1 after an underwhelming 28-15 win over Chatfield in Week 0. The Bruins extended their win streak to 28 games but face a significant test next week against No. 4 Ralston Valley, which opened the season with a 31-0 shutout of Castle View — setting up a rematch of last year's 5A championship game.

In an upset, No. 3 Legend fell 28-24 to No. 6 Grandview after leading 24-21 entering the fourth quarter, with Grandview's Blake Richmeier connecting with Lander Wise on a 40-yard touchdown pass for the decisive score. No. 5 Mountain Vista rallied from a 26-7 second-quarter deficit to beat No. 8 Arapahoe 43-39, with quarterback Marquise Reese scoring the go-ahead rushing touchdown with under 10 minutes remaining.

stories.headline: Denver Post launches Colorado Gold Softball Award for state's top high school senior
stories.summary:
The Denver Post announced the creation of the Colorado Gold Softball Award, a new annual honor that will be presented to the state's top high school senior softball player, scholar and community member. The inaugural award will be given at the conclusion of the CHSAA softball season in late October, in the 40th year of sanctioned Colorado high school softball.

Like the newspaper's existing Gold Helmet Award in football, Roy Halladay Award in baseball and April Heinrichs Award in girls soccer, the softball honor weighs academic performance and community service alongside on-field achievements. Finalists and the winner will be selected by a 23-person committee including coaches, media members and former players. The winner will receive a $1,000 scholarship, a trophy, a profile in The Denver Post and recognition at a Coors Field game next spring.

The award is backed by the nonprofit Colorado High School Softball Player Award Corporation and made possible by donations, including a major pledge from Arvada resident Adam Stevinson, who also helped fund the April Heinrichs Award. The board includes original Rockies employee Alan Bossart, longtime MLB scout Ed Henderson and prominent Colorado high school softball coaches including Eaglecrest's Yvette Hendrian and Valor Christian's Dave Atencio.

stories.headline: Colorado fall foliage forecast released for 2026 season
stories.summary:
Colorado's 2026 fall foliage forecast has been released, giving residents and visitors a guide to when and where leaves are expected to peak across the state. Colorful Colorado typically sees its first significant leaf changes in higher elevations in late August and early September, with color spreading to lower elevations and the Front Range through October.

The timing and intensity of fall color each year is influenced by summer rainfall, temperature swings and the onset of cooler nights. After a summer that included drought conditions and severe thunderstorms across parts of the state, forecasters are evaluating how stress on vegetation may affect the vibrancy and timing of the color change this year.

Leaf-peeping is a significant driver of fall tourism across Colorado, with popular destinations including Rocky Mountain National Park, the San Juan Mountains, Kebler Pass and the Maroon Bells near Aspen drawing large crowds each autumn.

stories.headline: Missing endangered 13-year-old girl last seen in north Denver, CBI issues alert
stories.summary:
The Colorado Bureau of Investigation has issued an endangered missing person alert for a 13-year-old girl last seen in the north Denver area. CBI activated the alert due to concerns for the girl's safety and wellbeing, though specific circumstances surrounding her disappearance have not been fully detailed in available reports.

Endangered missing person alerts in Colorado are issued when law enforcement believes a missing individual faces a credible threat to their life or safety. The CBI coordinates with local law enforcement agencies to publicize such alerts and gather tips from the public.

Anyone with information about the missing girl's whereabouts is urged to contact local law enforcement or the CBI tip line. Additional details, including a description and photograph, are expected to be distributed through official CBI channels.

stories.headline: Denver-based developer preserves 120 affordable apartments in Eagle, averting displacement of dozens of families
stories.summary:
A Denver-based developer has preserved 120 affordable housing units in Eagle, Colorado, preventing the potential displacement of dozens of lower-income families who reside there. The preservation effort keeps the units available at below-market rents at a time when housing costs across Colorado's mountain communities have surged dramatically, making affordable options increasingly scarce.

Affordable housing preservation — acquiring and maintaining existing below-market units rather than building new ones — has become a growing strategy for developers and municipalities seeking to prevent displacement in high-cost areas. Eagle County, like much of the Colorado mountain corridor, has seen significant pressure on workforce and affordable housing as remote workers and second-home buyers have driven up property values.

The project adds to a broader conversation in Colorado about the most effective tools for maintaining housing affordability, with preservation efforts often cited as faster and less expensive than new construction. Details about the specific financing mechanisms and long-term affordability restrictions attached to the Eagle units were not immediately available.

topStory.headline: USS Abraham Lincoln Passes Singapore Strait, Heads Home After Record-Length Middle East Deployment
topStory.summary:
The USS Abraham Lincoln, one of the U.S. Navy's largest warships, transited waters near Singapore early Sunday morning as it made its way home following a prolonged deployment in the Middle East. Associated Press journalists stationed on the Indonesian island of Batam observed the carrier passing through the Singapore Strait shortly after 1 a.m. local time. Thai officials have confirmed the vessel is expected to make a port stop in Thailand for rest and recovery before returning to its home base.

The Lincoln departed San Diego on Nov. 21 with a crew of approximately 5,000 sailors. The ship's deployment was significantly extended by the U.S. war against Iran, which began in February, ultimately resulting in a record-setting uninterrupted stretch at sea exceeding 250 days. The carrier served as a primary launch platform for thousands of aircraft sorties supporting strikes during the conflict. The Japan-based USS George Washington arrived in the Middle East earlier this month to relieve the Lincoln.

The extended deployment drew public attention after family members reported deteriorating conditions aboard the ship, including alleged food shortages, inadequate hygiene supplies, and declining mental health among crew members. Jefferson Kelley, whose son Jackson is serving aboard the Lincoln on his first deployment, told CBS Mornings that the sailors "should not be deployed this long" and described the strain on families waiting for their return. U.S. Central Command disputed reports of widespread suicidal ideation among the crew, stating there have been no deaths aboard the vessel.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth previously characterized media reports about conditions on the Lincoln as "misrepresented." The Navy confirmed that an Aug. 3 incident in which a sailor fell overboard and was recovered remains under investigation. The Lincoln's return marks the conclusion of what stands as one of the lengthiest continuous carrier deployments in recent U.S. naval history, and will renew scrutiny of the human and operational costs of the sustained military campaign against Iran.
